definition: Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) are a type of artificial neural network architecture inspired by the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem, also known as the superposition theorem.
details: Unlike traditional multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), which rely on fixed activation functions and linear weights, KANs replace each weight with a learnable univariate function, often represented using splines.

explainer.lead: Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks are a neural architecture built on the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem. They matter as an alternative to multilayer perceptrons with a different parameterisation of the network.

tiers.eli5: Instead of fixed knobs and fixed switches, the network learns the shape of each small function itself.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers replace each weight with a learnable univariate function, often represented with splines, instead of fixed activation functions and linear weights. The pitfall is that spline functions add per-edge complexity that must be managed.
tiers.paperLevel: Based on the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem, also called the superposition theorem; each weight in an MLP is replaced by a learnable univariate function, often spline-based.

explainer.example: A layer that would multiply an input by a weight in an MLP instead applies its own learned spline curve to that input before summing.
